To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ergodic MIMO channel capacity depends on the condition number of a matrix that is a function of the channel's spatial fading correlation, the scattering radii of the transmit and receive antennas, the distance between the antennas, and the beamwidth and spacing of the antennas.
the rank of a MIMO wireless channel is a strong function of scattering conditions and that, in general, high rank channels can be sustained over long ranges under mild scattering conditions.

the rank of the channel is governed by the condition number of a matrix that depends on the scattering environment and the antenna array parameters, that this matrix is related to the array manifold matrix, and that the rank is maximized when the scattering radii are equal to the antenna spacing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the modeling and performance prediction of outdoor MIMO wireless channels.
the characterization of MIMO channels, the prediction of channel capacity and rank properties, and the design of high-capacity MIMO systems.
developing a better understanding of MIMO channel capacity, and how to predict its behavior in realistic outdoor wireless scenarios.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ergodic capacity of MIMO wireless channels depends on the condition number of their channel matrices, and this in turn depends on the scattering conditions at both the transmitter and receiver, the distance between the transmitter and receiver arrays, and the beamwidth and inter-element spacing of the transmit and receive antennas.
, contrary to popular belief, MIMO capacity is not governed by the distance between the transmit/receive antennas, but rather, by the spatial fading correlation at the transmitter and receiver.
the ergodic capacity of a MIMO channel depends primarily on the scattering radii and the antenna spacing at both ends of a link.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ergodic capacity of a MIMO system depends not only on the number of antennas but also on the propagation environment, which can be controlled by the antenna design and the scattering environment at the transmitter and receiver.

the capacity of MIMO channels depends on the rank of the channel, which in turn depends on the spatial fading correlation at the transmitter and receiver and on the condition number of their scattering environments.
the MIMO performance is governed by the condition number of channel matrix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MIMO capacity is determined by the rank of the channel, and the spatial fading correlation is only a secondary effect.

the MIMO channel rank is governed not only by the scattering conditions at the transmitter, receiver and the distance between the transmit/receive antenna arrays, but also by their beamwidths and the antenna element spacing.
the MIMO capacity of outdoor channels is not necessarily a function of the distance alone.
